c-florentine-codex.text: The Florentine Codex, an encyclopedia in Nahuatl and Spanish compiled from the mid-16th century under the direction of the Franciscan missionary Bernardino de Sahagún, was completed in 1575-77; it has 12 books and 2,468 illustrations and is held in the Laurentian Library, Florence.
c-florentine-codex.label: consensus

c-slavevoyages-125m.text: The SlaveVoyages database, reflecting 34,948 voyages, underlies the estimate that some 12.5 million Africans were taken from their homes and forced aboard slave ships.
c-slavevoyages-125m.label: approx
c-slavevoyages-125m.note: 'Some 12.5 million' is an estimate built from the voyage records, not a count of individuals. The trade is the subject of 13.7.

c-orbis-spike.text: Simon Lewis and Mark Maslin (Nature, 2015) proposed that a pronounced dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide centred on 1610, recorded in Antarctic ice cores, followed the deaths of about 50 million Indigenous Americans after colonisation and the regrowth of forests; they called it the 'Orbis Spike'.
c-orbis-spike.label: debated
c-orbis-spike.note: A proposal, made partly to mark the start of a new geological epoch, the Anthropocene; it is examined on 13.5.

c-guamanpoma-chronicle.text: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's illustrated Andean chronicle, the Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (1612-15), is 'a critical account of Spanish rule in Peru'; it includes a prologue addressed to King Philip III, and the autograph manuscript is in the Royal Danish Library, Copenhagen.
c-guamanpoma-chronicle.label: consensus

c-dias-1488.text: Bartolomeu Dias probably left Portugal in August 1487; he rounded the Cape of Good Hope without having seen it and returned to Portugal in December 1488.
c-dias-1488.label: approx
c-dias-1488.note: The departure date is inferred: Britannica says it is 'now usually supposed' that he left in August 1487.

c-cape-name-dispute.text: Who named the Cape of Good Hope is uncertain: Barros says Dias named it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it, while Duarte Pacheco credits the name to Dias himself.
c-cape-name-dispute.label: debated
c-cape-name-dispute.note: Britannica judges Pacheco's version the likelier.

c-dagama-1498.text: Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon on 8 July 1497, rounded the Cape of Good Hope on 22 November, took on at Malindi a Gujarati pilot who knew the route to Calicut, and reached Calicut on 20 May 1498.
c-dagama-1498.label: consensus

c-dagama-calicut-gifts.text: At Calicut, in Britannica's words, the Zamorin's goodwill 'was dispelled by da Gama's insignificant gifts and rude behaviour.'
c-dagama-calicut-gifts.label: consensus

c-dagama-losses.text: Of da Gama's original crew of 170, only 55 survived the voyage; he reached Lisbon on 9 September 1499.
c-dagama-losses.label: consensus

c-tordesillas-1494.text: The Treaty of Tordesillas, made by Spain and Portugal on 7 June 1494, set the line between their claims 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, with lands to the east of it going to Portugal and those to the west to Spain; the pope's earlier line had been 100 leagues (about 320 miles) west of the islands.
c-tordesillas-1494.label: consensus

c-cabral-brazil-1500.text: Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted Brazil on 22 April 1500, naming it the Island of the True Cross, took formal possession, stayed 10 days, and reached Calicut on 13 September 1500; Dias, sailing in the same fleet, was lost at sea near the Cape of Good Hope.
c-cabral-brazil-1500.label: consensus

c-albuquerque-goa-melaka.text: Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa by assault in November 1510, when its Muslim defenders were put to the sword, and took Malacca (Melaka) in July 1511.
c-albuquerque-goa-melaka.label: consensus

c-albuquerque-fortresses.text: Albuquerque aimed to establish permanent fortresses with settled populations. After he captured Hormuz in August 1507, his project of building a fortress there had to be abandoned because of differences with his captains; in February 1515 he sailed again for Hormuz with 26 ships, gaining control of part of the island.
c-albuquerque-fortresses.label: consensus

c-goa-unesco-churches.text: UNESCO describes Goa as 'the former capital of the Portuguese Indies'; its churches, one of which holds the tomb of Francis Xavier, 'illustrate the evangelization of Asia'.
c-goa-unesco-churches.label: consensus

c-columbus-1492-voyage.text: Columbus's fleet left on 3 August 1492, and on 12 October land was sighted from the Pinta.
c-columbus-1492-voyage.label: consensus

c-guanahani-landfall.text: Where Columbus first landed, on the island called Guanahani, is hotly disputed, though San Salvador (Watling's Island) in the Bahamas is generally preferred.
c-guanahani-landfall.label: debated
c-guanahani-landfall.note: Britannica calls the identification 'hotly disputed'; no candidate has been proven.

c-columbus-asia-belief.text: Columbus convinced himself that Cuba was the Asian mainland, and he never abandoned the belief that he had reached Asia.
c-columbus-asia-belief.label: consensus

c-columbus-prophecies.text: After 1500 Columbus compiled a Book of Prophecies; its modern publisher describes it as presenting his voyages as 'a first step toward the liberation of Jerusalem'.
c-columbus-prophecies.label: consensus

c-columbus-delaney.text: Carol Delaney argues that Columbus sought gold to fund a crusade; a Publishers Weekly reviewer summarised her thesis as Columbus seeking 'to obtain enough of the fabled gold of the East to launch a crusade'.
c-columbus-delaney.label: debated
c-columbus-delaney.note: Delaney, Columbus and the Quest for Jerusalem. A Publishers Weekly reviewer objected that her reading 'provides thin evidence for her conclusions.'

c-navidad-1492.text: After the Santa María ran aground on 25 December 1492, Columbus built a fort, La Navidad, on Hispaniola with help from the Taíno chief Guacanagarí, and left 39 men to guard it.
c-navidad-1492.label: consensus

c-taino-people.text: The Taíno were an Arawakan-speaking people who, when Columbus arrived, inhabited the Greater Antilles, including what is now Cuba.
c-taino-people.label: consensus

c-taino-pop-estimates.text: Estimates of the Taíno population at contact differ widely: Britannica says the Taíno 'may have numbered one or two million'; Livi Bacci (2003) estimates 200,000-300,000 for Hispaniola; and a 2021 ancient-DNA study concludes that 'previous pan-Caribbean estimates of hundreds of thousands of people are too large'.
c-taino-pop-estimates.label: debated
c-taino-pop-estimates.note: Livi Bacci notes that earlier estimates for Hispaniola ran from 60,000 to 8 million. Fernandes, Sirak and colleagues estimate the combined effective population of Puerto Rico and Hispaniola at a maximum of 1,530-8,150 people in the generations before those sampled, and say census sizes are 'unlikely to be more than tenfold larger'; ten times their maximum is about 80,000, a calculation the authors do not state.

c-hispaniola-collapse.text: On Livi Bacci's figures, Hispaniola's Indigenous population had fallen to 60,000 by 1508 and to just over 26,000 in the repartimiento of 1514; after the smallpox epidemic of 1518-19 only a few thousand remained.
c-hispaniola-collapse.label: approx
c-hispaniola-collapse.note: Colonial counts analysed by Livi Bacci (2003); the starting figure they fell from is disputed.

c-livibacci-causes.text: Livi Bacci argues that 'the Tainos of the Antilles were on the verge of extinction before the first smallpox epidemics struck the islands in 1518', and attributes the collapse to conquest itself: gold mining, the encomienda, displacement and falling fertility.
c-livibacci-causes.label: debated
c-livibacci-causes.note: Livi Bacci (2003, 2006). The older explanation put epidemic disease first; he finds no proven deadly epidemics before 1518-19.

c-montesinos-1511.text: On the fourth Sunday of Advent 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached on Hispaniola against the colonists' treatment of the Indians, taking as his text 'I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness' and asking, in Las Casas's account as translated by Stafford Poole, 'Are they not men? Do they not have rational souls?'
c-montesinos-1511.label: consensus

c-burgos-1512.text: The Laws of Burgos (27 December 1512) required encomenderos to give the Indians religious instruction, food and clothing and banned whipping; Burkholder writes that they aimed to make exploitation 'just', and that in practice they did not improve conditions.
c-burgos-1512.label: consensus

c-lascasas-career.text: Bartolomé de las Casas sailed to the New World in 1502 with the expedition of Nicolás de Ovando, was later ordained a priest and became a leading critic of the colonists; Britannica calls him 'the first to expose the oppression of the Indian by the European'.
c-lascasas-career.label: approx
c-lascasas-career.note: Reference works disagree on when he was ordained: in Rome, after returning to Europe in 1507 (Lunenfeld); in 1510 (The Renaissance); about 1512 (Rooy); or in 1512 or 1513 (Donovan).

c-new-laws-1542.text: The New Laws of 1542-43 prohibited the enslavement of Indians, even as punishment, and stopped encomiendas passing to heirs; a revolt in Peru followed, in which the first viceroy was beheaded, and the ban on inheritance was repealed in 1545-46.
c-new-laws-1542.label: consensus

c-valladolid-1550.text: At the Junta of Valladolid in 1550-51 Las Casas debated Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda over whether Aristotle's idea of natural slavery applied to the Indians.
c-valladolid-1550.label: approx
c-valladolid-1550.note: González Fuxà (2023) dates it 'entre 1550 y 1551'; the Encyclopedia.com entry gives 1550 only.

c-fuxa-natural-slavery.text: José González Fuxà (2023) argues that 16th-century Spaniards read natural slavery in a broad sense, as an inferiority that education and faith could overcome, rather than as a fixed condition.
c-fuxa-natural-slavery.label: debated
c-fuxa-natural-slavery.note: New, in a doctoral thesis; Aristotle's natural slave is 'un hombre naturalmente incompleto', and the question is how literally Spaniards applied the idea.

c-lascasas-blacklegend.text: Las Casas's writings, among them A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552), were 'a major source of the "Black Legend"', and Spanish patriots condemned him for helping to create it. Two reference entries judge that he exaggerated Spanish cruelty or the numbers killed; Donovan, by contrast, writes that 'Modern scholarship has supported Las Casas's staggering toll of native deaths', while blaming them chiefly on disease, and that, whether or not he exaggerated, A Brief Account 'remains one of the most important documents ever written on human rights'.
c-lascasas-blacklegend.label: debated
c-lascasas-blacklegend.note: From the reference entries collected by Encyclopedia.com (Lunenfeld; Donovan; World Eras; American Eras). They also differ over African slavery: World Eras says he proposed using Africans as slave labourers in place of Native Americans but 'soon repented of that idea', while Donovan reports that recent work has refuted the claim that he promoted the African slave trade as a substitute for Indian slavery.

c-cortes-1519.text: Hernán Cortés landed at Tabasco in March 1519, founded Veracruz and sank his ships; a marker at Quiahuiztlán, on the Gulf coast, says that the settlement the Spaniards built nearby 'was called "Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz", and it is considered the first Spanish settlement in Mexico'.
c-cortes-1519.label: consensus

c-malintzin-marina.text: Malintzin, also called Doña Marina, became Cortés's mistress and interpreter and bore him a son.
c-malintzin-marina.label: consensus

c-tlaxcala-ally.text: Tlaxcala first resisted Cortés and then became his most faithful ally; on 8 November 1519 he entered Tenochtitlan with his small Spanish force and only 1,000 Tlaxcaltecs.
c-tlaxcala-ally.label: consensus

c-moctezuma-seized.text: Cortés soon seized Moctezuma, who died about 30 June 1520.
c-moctezuma-seized.label: approx
c-moctezuma-seized.note: Britannica gives the date as approximate.

c-smallpox-tenochtitlan.text: Smallpox reached Tenochtitlan in September or October 1520; it killed Moctezuma's successor, and an estimated one-third to one-half of the population died during the epidemic.
c-smallpox-tenochtitlan.label: approx
c-smallpox-tenochtitlan.note: Bonnie L. Ford's estimate, which does not say whether it covers the city alone or a wider region. Some chroniclers name the carrier as Francisco Eguía, a member of the force sent to arrest Cortés.

c-tenochtitlan-fall-1521.text: The capture of Tenochtitlan was completed on 13 August 1521.
c-tenochtitlan-fall-1521.label: consensus

c-florentine-book12.text: Book 12 of the Florentine Codex tells the conquest from the Mexica side, with chapters on the massacre at Cholula, the meeting of Moctezuma and Cortés, and the plague that struck Tenochtitlan.
c-florentine-book12.label: consensus

c-restall-myths.text: Matthew Restall treats the heroic story of Spanish superiority as a myth: he argues that the conquest 'relied heavily on black and native allies', and that Indigenous people saw it 'as a native civil war in which the Spaniards played an important but secondary role.'
c-restall-myths.label: debated
c-restall-myths.note: Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003; later edition). His target is the heroic narrative of Prescott and others, which gave the decisive role to the Spaniards.

c-inca-civilwar.text: After the death of Huayna Capac his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fought a civil war, by one account for seven years, 'turning the empire's armies against each other'; Atahualpa had won by 1532, just as Pizarro arrived.
c-inca-civilwar.label: approx
c-inca-civilwar.note: The seven-year length is McKay and colleagues' figure.

c-cajamarca-1532.text: At Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 Francisco Pizarro's force of about 168 Spaniards seized Atahualpa.
c-cajamarca-1532.label: approx
c-cajamarca-1532.note: The figure of 168 is World History Encyclopedia's, following D'Altroy; Britannica gives 180 men for the expedition's departure from Panama.

c-atahualpa-ransom-death.text: Atahualpa fulfilled a promise to fill the room where he was held with gold and silver, but he was executed by strangling in 1533; the sources disagree on the date.
c-atahualpa-ransom-death.label: debated
c-atahualpa-ransom-death.note: Britannica gives 29 August 1533. World History Encyclopedia gives 26 July 1533, and says a sentence of burning was commuted to strangulation after he was baptized.

c-cuzco-lima.text: Cuzco was occupied without a struggle in November 1533; Pizarro founded Lima in 1535 and was killed by Almagro's former supporters on 26 June 1541.
c-cuzco-lima.label: consensus

c-potosi-silver-mita.text: Silver was found at the Cerro Rico of Potosí between 1542 and 1545; UNESCO says Potosí was 'reputed to be the world's largest industrial complex in the 16th century', and that workers were forced to labour in its mines under the mita, a system of mandatory labour.
c-potosi-silver-mita.label: approx
c-potosi-silver-mita.note: UNESCO gives a span of years for the discovery rather than a single date.

c-dell-mita-effects.text: The mining mita was in force in Peru and Bolivia from 1573 to 1812. Comparing districts on either side of its old boundary, Melissa Dell (2010) found that a former mita district today has household consumption about 25 percent lower and child stunting about 6 percentage points higher.
c-dell-mita-effects.label: debated
c-dell-mita-effects.note: Dell, Econometrica (2010). A 2025 preprint by Karakas, not yet peer-reviewed, re-estimates the effects with machine-learning methods and reports them larger and varying from place to place.

c-guadalupe-tradition.text: According to tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin at Tepeyac on 9-12 December 1531, and her image appeared on his tilma before Bishop Zumárraga.
c-guadalupe-tradition.label: tradition
c-guadalupe-tradition.note: The account as Catholic tradition tells it; for when it was first written down, see the next claim.

c-juandiego-canonized.text: John Paul II canonized Juan Diego in Mexico City on 31 July 2002, praising him for 'accepting the Christian message without forgoing his indigenous identity'.
c-juandiego-canonized.label: consensus

c-guadalupe-written-record.text: The first published accounts of the Guadalupe apparitions are Miguel Sánchez's (1648) and Luis Laso de la Vega's Nahuatl text (1649), more than a century after the date the tradition gives.
c-guadalupe-written-record.label: debated
c-guadalupe-written-record.note: Stafford Poole judges that the symbolism 'does not rest on any objective historical basis'. Upholders of the tradition, Timothy Matovina writes, 'argue, or simply presume, that Sánchez's publication is based on oral testimony' or on an earlier unpublished version of the narrative.

c-guadalupe-tonantzin.text: Sánchez himself identified Tepeyac as a pre-Christian pilgrimage site of the goddess Tonantzin, and held that Guadalupe had providentially taken Tonantzin's place in the natives' devotion; Sahagún 'opposed Guadalupan devotion as a thinly-veiled continuation of indigenous religion and worship'.
c-guadalupe-tonantzin.label: debated
c-guadalupe-tonantzin.note: As set out by Timothy Matovina (2003): Sánchez saw Guadalupe as replacing Tonantzin, Sahagún saw the devotion as continuing Indigenous worship.

c-gd-pop1492.text: A 2019 synthesis of regional estimates by Koch and colleagues gives a pre-1492 population for the Americas of 60.5 million.
c-gd-pop1492.label: approx
c-gd-pop1492.note: One estimate among several; Chapter 12 sets out the range (12.11).

c-gd-loss90.text: The same study, which speaks of a 'Great Dying', estimates that European epidemics removed 90 percent (interquartile range 87-92 percent) of the Indigenous population over the following century.
c-gd-loss90.label: approx
c-gd-loss90.note: A model-based estimate. Its wording puts epidemics first; for other causes see Reséndez and the 2026 burial study on this page.

c-gd-brit-range.text: Britannica gives a wider range: across the Americas, populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, and on most Caribbean islands the Native population fell by more than 99 percent.
c-gd-brit-range.label: approx
c-gd-brit-range.note: A range, because both the starting populations and the later counts are uncertain estimates.

c-gd-diseases.text: Europeans brought diseases new to the Americas, among them measles, smallpox, influenza, mumps, typhus and whooping cough.
c-gd-diseases.label: consensus

c-gd-resendez.text: Andrés Reséndez (The Other Slavery, 2016) argues that slavery, overwork and famine, not only disease, drove the collapse, and estimates that between 2.5 and 5 million Native Americans were enslaved between the time of Columbus and 1900.
c-gd-resendez.label: debated
c-gd-resendez.note: His Kirkus reviewer notes that the extinction of Indigenous peoples 'is usually written off as the effect of diseases'; Reséndez's reply, in the reviewer's words: 'They died from slavery, overwork, and famine.' Koch et al.'s wording, by contrast, puts epidemics first.

c-gd-burials.text: A 2026 study led by Alex Garcia-Putnam in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology notes that 'there are no documented mass or altered burials identified as resulting from smallpox during the colonial period', and proposes criteria to guide future research.
c-gd-burials.label: debated
c-gd-burials.note: New (2026). It proposes criteria for evaluating burials and skeletal remains. Nicole Smith-Guzman of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute is quoted: 'It wasn't just diseases as biological agents that were affecting people's health.'

c-gd-cocoliztli.text: Ancient DNA from 10 of 24 individuals sampled from a cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca linked to the cocoliztli epidemic of 1545-1550 contained the bacterium Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, which the researchers present as a possible cause of the epidemic; five pre-contact burials from the same site tested negative.
c-gd-cocoliztli.label: debated
c-gd-cocoliztli.note: Vågene et al. (2018), known here from the press release, which speaks of 'a possible cause', not a proven one.

c-gd-crosby.text: The phrase 'the Columbian Exchange' comes from the title of Alfred W. Crosby's 1972 book.
c-gd-crosby.label: consensus

c-gd-crops.text: American staples such as maize, potatoes, cassava and sweet potatoes spread to the Old World; maize had the biggest impact, altering agriculture in Asia, Europe and Africa, and cassava was introduced to Africa in the 16th century.
c-gd-crops.label: consensus

c-gd-livestock.text: Old World livestock, cattle and horses especially, ran wild and reproduced prolifically on the Pampas and the Great Plains.
c-gd-livestock.label: consensus

c-gd-orbis.text: Simon Lewis and Mark Maslin (Nature, 2015) proposed that the Anthropocene probably began around 1610, at a dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide they called the 'Orbis Spike', which they attribute directly to the arrival of Europeans in the Americas.
c-gd-orbis.label: debated
c-gd-orbis.note: A proposed start date, known here from the UCL press release. The release puts the Indigenous deaths at about 50 million, fewer than the roughly 54 million (90 percent of 60.5 million) implied by Koch et al. No Anthropocene epoch has been adopted; in 2024 geologists rejected a proposal that would have dated it to the mid-20th century.

c-gd-regrowth.text: Koch et al. calculate that regrowth on 55.8 million hectares of abandoned land in the Americas was equivalent to a fall in atmospheric carbon dioxide of 3.5 parts per million; accounting for carbon-cycle feedbacks and land-use change outside the Americas gives a total of 5 ppm of additional uptake, 47-67 percent of the observed fall of 7-10 parts per million. They find that the carbon budget of the 1500s cannot be balanced without large-scale regrowth in the Americas.
c-gd-regrowth.label: debated
c-gd-regrowth.note: Model estimates with wide ranges (the land area could be 39.0-78.4 million hectares, the direct effect 2.3-5.1 ppm). On these figures regrowth was a large part of the fall, but not all of it.

c-anthropocene-2024.text: In March 2024 the International Union of Geological Sciences announced 'a decisive rejection of the Anthropocene proposal: 4 votes in favour; 12 votes against; and 3 abstentions'; the rejected proposal had a mid-20th-century start date, and the IUGS said that the Anthropocene will not be recognised as a formal geological term.
c-anthropocene-2024.label: consensus

c-ag-potosi.text: Silver was discovered at Potosí, in the Andes, between 1542 and 1545, and in the 16th century the site was regarded as the world's largest industrial complex.
c-ag-potosi.label: approx
c-ag-potosi.note: UNESCO's Dutch-language text gives the discovery as 'tussen 1542 en 1545', between 1542 and 1545.

c-ag-zacatecas.text: Zacatecas, in New Spain, was founded in 1546 after the discovery of a rich silver lode.
c-ag-zacatecas.label: consensus

c-ag-150k.text: Spanish America was the source of approximately 150,000 tons of silver between 1500 and 1800, perhaps 80 percent of world production.
c-ag-150k.label: approx
c-ag-150k.note: Flynn and Giráldez's estimate, as cited by Carlos Marichal, who writes 'perhaps 80%'.

c-ag-flynn.text: Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez argue that global trade emerged with the founding of Manila in 1571, and that silver flowed to China because its value there surged to double its worth in the rest of the world.
c-ag-flynn.label: debated
c-ag-flynn.note: Flynn and Giráldez (1995). Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson, who measure globalization by the convergence of commodity prices, place the 'very big globalization bang' in the 19th century; they do not discuss 1571 directly.

c-ag-orourke.text: Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson treat commodity price convergence as 'the central manifestation of globalization'; they find 'no evidence supporting the view that the world economy was globally integrated prior to 1492 and/or 1498', and conclude that 'the 19th century contained a very big globalization bang'.
c-ag-orourke.label: debated
c-ag-orourke.note: O'Rourke and Williamson (2000). Their paper does not discuss 1571 directly; the contrast with Flynn and Giráldez, who use a different test, the flow of silver to China, is ours.

c-ag-galleon.text: Through the 17th century the Manila galleons carried on average about two million pesos of silver a year, more than fifty tons, from Acapulco to Manila, which was little more than a way station for Spanish silver on its way to China.
c-ag-galleon.label: approx
c-ag-galleon.note: A 17th-century average, given by Peter Coclanis, who attributes it to Flynn and Giráldez.

c-ag-singlewhip.text: Ming China's 'single whip' reform, promulgated throughout the empire in 1581, reduced land tax and labour service to a single payment in silver.
c-ag-singlewhip.label: debated
c-ag-singlewhip.note: Britannica judges it 'little more than a bookkeeping change at best' and says it was not universally applied. EBSCO's Research Starter stresses that it 'was made possible only through China's dependence on foreign silver'.

c-ag-navarrus.text: Martín de Azpilcueta, known as Navarrus, of the School of Salamanca, set out an early quantity theory of money in his Comentario (1556) and is considered an independent discoverer of the theory.
c-ag-navarrus.label: consensus

c-ag-hamilton.text: In 1934 Earl Hamilton argued that imports of American treasure were the principal cause of the price revolution in Spain.
c-ag-hamilton.label: debated
c-ag-hamilton.note: John Munro objects that the price revolution 'had begun as early as the quinquennium 1516-20', before large silver imports. Other explanations stress population growth or, in the models of Harry Miskimin and Jack Goldstone, a rising velocity of money.

c-ag-isotopes.text: Isotope studies of coins point in different directions. In a study of coins from Europe and the Americas, Anne-Marie Desaulty and colleagues found that 'Mexican silver did not enter Spanish coinage from the 16th century to the beginning of the 17th century', and Desaulty said that the results 'call into question the secular idea that the "prices revolution" is related to the massive arrival of American metals'. In another, Desaulty and Francis Albarède found Mexican silver in English coins from around the mid-1550s, but silver from Potosí only nearly a century later; Science News reported that this study 'adds hard data to theories linking the transatlantic influx of silver to price inflation'.
c-ag-isotopes.label: debated
c-ag-isotopes.note: Reported by Chemistry World and by Science News (2012), which adds that it is 'not yet clear whether these particular English coins reflect a larger trend across Europe'.

c-st-total.text: The SlaveVoyages database estimates that about 12.5 million Africans were shipped to the Americas and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage.
c-st-total.label: approx
c-st-total.note: Model-based estimates from voyage records, as reported by Henry Louis Gates Jr. Britannica gives a lower total, between 10 million and 12 million.

c-st-century.text: By century, the database estimates that 277,506 people were embarked in 1501-1600, 1,875,631 in 1601-1700, 6,494,619 in 1701-1800 and 3,873,580 in 1801-1866: 12,521,336 embarked and 10,702,656 landed in all.
c-st-century.label: approx
c-st-century.note: SlaveVoyages estimates (2009 version) as tabulated by Macmillan Learning; exact-looking numbers for what are estimates, not counts. Macmillan's table prints 227,506 for 1501-1600, a misprint: its century rows add up to its stated total only with 277,506, and a regional tabulation of the same database in the IZA Journal of Development and Migration gives 277,505 for 1501-1600.

c-st-dest.text: Of those landed, about 51.9 percent went to the Caribbean, 38.9 percent to Brazil, 3.8 percent to North America and 3.3 percent to the Spanish American mainland; Gates puts the number brought to North America at about 388,000.
c-st-dest.label: approx
c-st-dest.note: Shares of the database's estimated arrivals, as tabulated by Macmillan Learning.

c-st-coast.text: An estimated 10 to 15 percent of captives died on their way to the African coast.
c-st-coast.label: approx

c-st-sugar.text: Demand for enslaved labour rose sharply with the growth of sugar plantations in the Caribbean.
c-st-sugar.label: consensus

c-st-afonso.text: In 1526 Afonso I (Nzinga Mbemba), the Christian king of Kongo, complained to King João III of Portugal that 'so great, Sir, is the corruption and licentiousness that our country is being completely depopulated'.
c-st-afonso.label: consensus

c-st-agaja.text: Agaja, king of Dahomey, took the kingdom of Allada in 1724 and the coastal trading state of Whydah (Ouidah) in 1727, and accepted the slave trade, though he insisted on a royal monopoly; whether he had earlier opposed it is disputed.
c-st-agaja.label: debated
c-st-agaja.note: Britannica says he 'gave up his opposition to the slave trade'. That opposition rests on I. A. Akinjogbin's thesis: David Henige and Marion Johnson (1976), re-examining the evidence, conclude that 'the motives and mechanisms of all parties were more complex than generally assumed', and David Ross (1989) writes that 'Akinjogbin's addenda have been shown to be at odds with the evidence'.

c-st-asiento.text: From the early 16th to the mid-18th century the Spanish crown granted asientos, agreements giving a private person or another power a monopoly on supplying African slaves to its American colonies; the last and most notable went to Britain's South Sea Company in 1713, under the Treaty of Utrecht, and entitled it to send 4,800 slaves to Spanish America a year for 30 years.
c-st-asiento.label: consensus

c-st-nunn.text: Nathan Nunn finds that the African countries from which the most slaves were taken are poorer today, and concludes that 'the slave trades have had an adverse effect on economic development'.
c-st-nunn.label: debated
c-st-nunn.note: Nunn (2008). Margherita Bottero and Björn Wallace (2013) reply that the relationship 'did not become significantly negative until 1970'.

c-ref-theses.text: On 31 October 1517, by the traditional account, Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses at the castle church in Wittenberg.
c-ref-theses.label: tradition
c-ref-theses.note: UNESCO repeats the traditional account. That he sent the theses to Archbishop Albrecht is certain; whether he posted them on the church door is debated.

c-ref-nailing.text: In a lecture at Mainz in 1961 the historian Erwin Iserloh argued that the nailing of the theses never happened; it is certain that Luther sent them to Archbishop Albrecht.
c-ref-nailing.label: debated
c-ref-nailing.note: Iserloh (1961). UNESCO's description of Wittenberg still follows the traditional account.

c-ref-print.text: Jared Rubin finds that cities with a printing press by 1500 were at minimum 29 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600.
c-ref-print.label: debated
c-ref-print.note: Rubin (2014) is a statistical study; how far printing caused the Reformation's spread is debated (13.12).

c-ref-anabaptists.text: On 21 January 1525, at the home of Felix Manz near the Grossmünster in Zurich, radicals who had broken with the reformer Ulrich Zwingli baptized each other, beginning the Anabaptist movement.
c-ref-anabaptists.label: approx
c-ref-anabaptists.note: Mennonite World Conference places the first baptisms at Felix Manz's home 'near the Grossmünster'; Christianity Today, cited for the date, says 'in a nearby village', apparently conflating them with the Zollikon baptisms that followed.

c-ref-calvin.text: In 1541 John Calvin's Ecclesiastical Ordinances defined the organisation of the Reformed church in Geneva.
c-ref-calvin.label: consensus

c-ref-supremacy.text: The Act of Supremacy of 1534 defined the right of Henry VIII to be supreme head on earth of the Church of England.
c-ref-supremacy.label: consensus

c-ref-jesuits.text: On 27 September 1540 Pope Paul III's bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae recognised the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, as a religious order.
c-ref-jesuits.label: consensus

c-ref-trent.text: The Council of Trent, meeting in three periods between 1545 and 1563, issued dogmatic definitions that clarified virtually every doctrine contested by Protestants.
c-ref-trent.label: consensus

c-ref-augsburg.text: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) left the rulers of the Empire's territories only two choices of confession, Roman Catholic or Lutheran, allowed dissenters to emigrate, and made no provision for other Protestants such as Calvinists.
c-ref-augsburg.label: consensus

c-ref-30yw.text: Peter H. Wilson estimates that around 1.8 million soldiers and at least 3.2 million civilians died in the Thirty Years' War, reducing the Empire's population by at least a fifth.
c-ref-30yw.label: approx
c-ref-30yw.note: Wilson's estimate; his own wording is 'around' and 'at least'.

c-ref-wilson-religion.text: Wilson argues that 'the Thirty Years War was neither inevitable nor a religious conflict'.
c-ref-wilson-religion.label: debated
c-ref-wilson-religion.note: Wilson's thesis, which runs against calling it simply a war of religion.

c-ref-westphalia.text: The Peace of Westphalia (1648), negotiated at Münster and Osnabrück, extended the Peace of Augsburg's toleration to the Reformed (Calvinist) church and confirmed the United Provinces of the Netherlands and the Swiss Confederation as independent republics.
c-ref-westphalia.label: consensus

c-ref-sovereignty.text: Britannica says the Peace of Westphalia recognised the full territorial sovereignty of the Empire's member states, and some scholars of international relations credit the treaties with providing the foundation of the modern state system.
c-ref-sovereignty.label: debated
c-ref-sovereignty.note: Andreas Osiander (2001) argues that international relations judges the present against 'a past that is largely imaginary', a product of the 19th- and 20th-century fixation on sovereignty.

c-ref-jews.text: In On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) Luther recommended setting fire to synagogues; in 1994 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America declared, 'we reject this violent invective'.
c-ref-jews.label: consensus

c-ref-gritsch.text: Eric Gritsch judged that Luther's 'arguments against Jews were theological, not biological', while noting that 'National Socialists used Luther to support their racist anti-Semitism'; the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America declared in 1994, 'we particularly deplore the appropriation of Luther's words by modern anti-Semites'.
c-ref-gritsch.label: debated
c-ref-gritsch.note: Gritsch's interpretation (1993), about the nature of Luther's hostility; it does not deny the violence of what Luther urged.

c-hs-philip.text: In 1555 Philip II assumed rule over his father's dominions; he made Madrid his capital, built the Escorial as his residence and the centre of his empire, and, never again leaving the Iberian peninsula, ruled his empire from his desk.
c-hs-philip.label: consensus

c-hs-1557.text: In 1557 the Spanish state was declared bankrupt, and not for the last time.
c-hs-1557.label: consensus

c-hs-dv.text: Philip II stopped all payments to his lenders four times; Mauricio Drelichman and Hans-Joachim Voth argue that these lending moratoria were sustained through a 'cheat the cheater' mechanism, in which lending remained profitable for the bankers overall.
c-hs-dv.label: debated
c-hs-dv.note: Drelichman and Voth's interpretation of the loan contracts; the paper adds that 'lending was profitable'.

c-hs-armada.text: The Armada that Philip II sent against England in 1588 was made up of some 130 to 150 ships and 18,000 men; after an English fireship attack off Calais and the fiercest fighting of the campaign at Gravelines, only about 65 ships returned to Spain.
c-hs-armada.label: approx
c-hs-armada.note: Rounded figures: Royal Museums Greenwich gives 'roughly 150 ships', Britannica 'about 130 ships'. Royal Museums Greenwich says the 65 'returned to Lisbon', but Medina Sidonia wrote to Philip II from Santander on 23 September 1588: 'Eight ships have entered this port, and five or six others, with Miguel de Oquendo, have run for the Biscay coast.'

c-hs-moriscos.text: Between 1609 and 1614 approximately 300,000 Moriscos, new Christians converted from Islam, were expelled from Spain, about 120,000 of them from Valencia; most settled in North Africa and Constantinople.
c-hs-moriscos.label: approx

c-hs-quixote.text: Miguel de Cervantes, honoured by UNESCO as the 'great son' of Alcalá de Henares, published Don Quixote in two parts, in 1605 and 1615.
c-hs-quixote.label: consensus

c-hs-teresa.text: Teresa of Ávila (1515-1582), born at Ávila, originated the Carmelite Reform, was canonised in 1622 and in 1970 was made a Doctor of the Church by Pope Paul VI, the first woman so honoured.
c-hs-teresa.label: consensus

c-hs-contemp.text: Contemporaries themselves wrote tracts speculating on why Spanish power had diminished.
c-hs-contemp.label: consensus

c-hs-elliott.text: History Today counts J. H. Elliott's 1961 essay 'The Decline of Spain' as one of 'the two best introductions' to the question, and his work addressed the attempts made by the country's leaders to avert its decline.
c-hs-elliott.label: debated
c-hs-elliott.note: Elliott treats decline as a problem Spain's own leaders saw and tried to meet; Henry Kamen questions the framing itself.

c-hs-kamen.text: Henry Kamen argues that politicians and historians of the 19th and 20th centuries, anxious to create a national identity, sought its roots 'in a fictitious image of what Spain was during the sixteenth century', and he examines 'the persistent obsession with the notion of national decline'.
c-hs-kamen.label: debated
c-hs-kamen.note: Kamen, Imagining Spain (2008), as described in the book's summary. Elliott's work, by contrast, treats decline as a problem that Spain's own leaders recognised.

c-suleyman-reign.text: Süleyman, known in Turkish as Kanuni ('the Lawgiver'), was sultan of the Ottoman empire from 1520 to 1566.
c-suleyman-reign.label: consensus

c-vienna-1529.text: In 1529 Süleyman laid siege to Vienna, but the siege was lifted.
c-vienna-1529.label: consensus

c-vienna-1683.text: A second Ottoman siege of Vienna, from 17 July to 12 September 1683, was broken by a relief army under Charles of Lorraine and the Polish king Jan III Sobieski.
c-vienna-1683.label: consensus

c-vienna-meaning.text: Britannica judges that the Ottoman defeat at Vienna in 1683 'marked the beginning of the end of Ottoman domination in eastern Europe'.
c-vienna-meaning.label: debated
c-vienna-meaning.note: An interpretation made with hindsight by Britannica's editors, not a fact about 1683 itself.

c-sabbatai-1665.text: Sabbatai Zevi, who had proclaimed himself the messiah at the age of 22, was wildly acclaimed at Smyrna (Izmir) in the autumn of 1665; Nathan of Gaza 'assumed the role of a modern Elijah', the movement spread to Venice, Amsterdam, Hamburg and London, and it threatened rabbinical authority.
c-sabbatai-1665.label: consensus

c-sabbatai-1666.text: In 1666, at Adrianople (Edirne), Sabbatai Zevi converted to Islam.
c-sabbatai-1666.label: consensus

c-safavid-1501.text: In July 1501 Ismail was enthroned as shah, his control at first limited to Azerbaijan; he 'proclaimed Shiʿism the state religion and enforced its creed and prayers in the mosques of his dominion'.
c-safavid-1501.label: consensus

c-ismail-tabriz.text: In 1501 Ismail took the city of Tabriz and proclaimed himself shah.
c-ismail-tabriz.label: consensus

c-chaldiran-1514.text: In August 1514 Ismail was seriously defeated at Chaldiran by his Sunni rival, the Ottoman sultan Selim I.
c-chaldiran-1514.label: consensus

c-abbas-isfahan.text: Abbas I, who came to the throne in 1588 and died in 1629, moved the capital to Isfahan and made it the centre of Safavid architectural achievement; Isfahan fell to the Ghilzai Afghans of Kandahar in 1722.
c-abbas-isfahan.label: consensus

c-akbar-policy.text: Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605. Rajput rulers concluded marriage alliances with him, and he reduced discrimination against non-Muslims by 'abolishing the taxation of pilgrims and the tax payable by non-Muslims in lieu of military service'.
c-akbar-policy.label: consensus

c-akbar-debates.text: Akbar never renounced Islam but took an active interest in other religions, persuading Hindus, Parsis and Christians, as well as Muslims, to engage in religious discussion before him. Building of a debating hall, the Ibadat Khana, began at Fatehpur Sikri early in 1575; it was meant to 'accommodate a large number of Muslim theologians', began as a Sunni and then a pan-Muslim assembly, and was opened to other religions when the discussions resumed in 1578.
c-akbar-debates.label: consensus

c-taj-mahal.text: The Taj Mahal was built at Agra between 1631 or 1632 and 1648, by order of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
c-taj-mahal.label: approx
c-taj-mahal.note: UNESCO's page gives the start of construction as 1631 in one place and 1632 in another.

c-aurangzeb-rule.text: Under Aurangzeb, emperor from 1658 to 1707, the Mughal empire reached its greatest extent and the two Muslim kingdoms of the Deccan were reduced to near-subjection; he reimposed the jizya, a poll tax on non-Muslims, in 1679, and Hindu idols, temples and shrines were often destroyed.
c-aurangzeb-rule.label: consensus

c-aurangzeb-legacy.text: Audrey Truschke (2017) sets out to discard the popular image of Aurangzeb, arguing that his temple destruction and persecution served political rather than religious purposes and fitted the sensibilities of his era.
c-aurangzeb-legacy.label: debated
c-aurangzeb-legacy.note: Reviewing her book, Shaharyar Zia finds some claims debatable, such as that Aurangzeb had 'no overarching agenda' regarding Hindus, given his reimposition of the jizya. Britannica judges that he left the empire 'not yet moribund' but facing 'a number of menacing problems'.

c-gunpowder-term.text: The historians William H. McNeill and Marshall G. S. Hodgson called the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal states 'gunpowder empires'.
c-gunpowder-term.label: consensus

c-gunpowder-critics.text: Recent historians have argued that the term 'gunpowder empires' may be misleading: despite having some firearms, most of these armies continued to rely mainly on swords, spears and bows, and the rulers' power may have rested more on advances in governance and global historical trends.
c-gunpowder-critics.label: debated
c-gunpowder-critics.note: As summarised by Trevor Getz (OER Project). Others, such as Douglas Streusand (2011), keep the label but reframe it.

c-agoston-firearms.text: Gábor Ágoston (2014) stresses the Ottomans' 'continued flexibility and pragmatism in adapting and improving on acquired weapons', alongside other factors such as good intelligence, resourceful leadership and large, disciplined professional armies.
c-agoston-firearms.label: debated
c-agoston-firearms.note: From the article's abstract. Ágoston gives gunpowder a real role in Ottoman military superiority, but not the only one.

c-streusand.text: Douglas Streusand (2011) keeps the label but depicts the three empires as part of an integrated international system, and as complex polities in which Islam is one political and cultural component among many.
c-streusand.label: debated
c-streusand.note: From the publisher's synopsis of his book Islamic Gunpowder Empires.

c-li-1644.text: In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing easily; a combined force of former Ming and Manchu troops then drove him from the capital.
c-li-1644.label: consensus

c-qing-1636.text: The Qing dynasty was first established in 1636 by the Manchus.
c-qing-1636.label: consensus

c-qing-growth.text: Under the Qing, China's territory grew to treble its size and its population grew from some 150 million to 450 million.
c-qing-growth.label: approx
c-qing-growth.note: Round figures from Britannica, which gives no years for them.

c-ming-megadrought.text: Tree rings show 'persistent megadroughts from 1576 to 1593 CE and from 1628 to 1644 CE in northern China', which Chen and colleagues (2024) argue contributed to the fall of the Ming.
c-ming-megadrought.label: debated
c-ming-megadrought.note: New research (Science Bulletin, 2024). The authors say the droughts 'contributed'; they do not claim drought alone brought down the dynasty, and how much weight climate should carry beside rebellion and politics is open.

c-kangxi-wars.text: The Kangxi emperor, second emperor of the Qing (reigned 1661-1722), defeated the Revolt of the Three Feudatories begun by Wu Sangui, his army entering Kunming in 1681; in 1683 he sent troops across the Taiwan Strait against the Zheng family, and in 1689 he concluded the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia.
c-kangxi-wars.label: consensus

c-kangxi-catholic.text: Kangxi encouraged the introduction of Western education and arts and of Roman Catholicism.
c-kangxi-catholic.label: consensus

c-ricci.text: The Jesuit Matteo Ricci arrived at Macau in August 1582, took a Confucian friend's advice to dress as a Chinese scholar, entered Beijing in January 1601 and stayed there until his death on 11 May 1610; he made the first edition of the 'Great Map of Ten Thousand Countries'.
c-ricci.label: consensus

c-rites.text: In the Chinese Rites Controversy, the Jesuits held that ceremonies honouring Confucius and family ancestors 'could be tolerated within certain limits', while the Dominicans and Franciscans opposed them and carried the issue to Rome; Clement XI banned the rites by a decree of 1704 and a bull of 1715, Benedict XIV reaffirmed the ban in 1742, and a decree of 1939 allowed Catholics to take part in ceremonies honouring Confucius.
c-rites.label: consensus

c-imjin-invasion.text: In 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea as part of his 'long-held plan to invade China through Korea'; his army captured Seoul on 12 June 1592.
c-imjin-invasion.label: consensus

c-imjin-war.text: Ming China sent armies to support Korea, and Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy, which included a few covered 'turtle-ships', hampered Japanese movements by sea; the invasion was abandoned after Hideyoshi died on 18 September 1598.
c-imjin-war.label: consensus

c-imjin-cost.text: The invasions caused the deaths of at least 125,000 Koreans, and many Korean potters were forcibly relocated to Japan; diplomatic and trade relations resumed in 1607.
c-imjin-cost.label: approx
c-imjin-cost.note: 'At least 125,000' is the figure given by Mark Cartwright in World History Encyclopedia, a popular source; the full toll is not known.

c-tokugawa.text: The Tokugawa shogunate, founded by Tokugawa Ieyasu and governing from Edo, lasted from 1603 to 1867, a period Britannica describes as one of 'internal peace, political stability, and economic growth'.
c-tokugawa.label: consensus

c-exclusion-decrees.text: Three exclusion decrees in the 1630s brought a complete ban on Christianity in Japan.
c-exclusion-decrees.label: consensus

c-four-portals.text: Arano Yasunori argues that Japan kept relations with the outside world through 'not one but four portals': after the exclusion of Portuguese ships (1639), the Dutch trading post was moved in 1641 from Hirado to Dejima, off Nagasaki, where Chinese merchants also traded; 'the Sō clan of Tsushima handled affairs with Korea'; 'the Shimazu clan of Satsuma was in charge of relations with Ryūkyū'; and the Matsumae domain oversaw contact with 'Ezo, the land of the Ainu'.
c-four-portals.label: debated
c-four-portals.note: Arano's case against the idea of 'national seclusion' (sakoku); he says the four-portals idea is now 'virtually standard terminology in Japanese history textbooks'.

c-toby-sakoku.text: Ronald Toby (State and Diplomacy in Early Modern Japan, 1984) challenged the idea of a policy of sakoku that 'closed' Japan, showing that the regime 'maintained an active network of information acquisition'.
c-toby-sakoku.label: debated
c-toby-sakoku.note: The older picture survives in reference works: Britannica still speaks of a policy of 'national seclusion'.

c-copernicus.text: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish astronomer, proposed that the planets have the Sun as the fixed point of their motions; his De revolutionibus was printed by Johann Petreius at Nuremberg in 1543, and he died at Frauenburg (Frombork) on 24 May 1543.
c-copernicus.label: consensus

c-osiander.text: De revolutionibus carried an unsigned letter by Andreas Osiander, whose role was not publicly revealed until Kepler did so in his Astronomia Nova (1609); Osiander also 'subtly changed the title to make it appear less like a claim of the real world'.
c-osiander.label: consensus

c-copernicus-deathbed.text: Copernicus is said to have received a copy of the printed book for the first time on his deathbed.
c-copernicus-deathbed.label: tradition
c-copernicus-deathbed.note: MacTutor reports this as a story ('is said to'), not as an attested fact.

c-galileo-moons.text: In January 1610 Galileo discovered four moons revolving around Jupiter, which he announced in Sidereus Nuncius.
c-galileo-moons.label: consensus

c-index-1616.text: A decree of the Congregation of the Index in 1616 declared false any theory that the Earth revolved around the Sun and ordered Copernicus's book 'suspended until they be corrected'; Decree XXI, 'finally issued in 1620, announced about a dozen corrections'.
c-index-1616.label: consensus

c-galileo-1633.text: Galileo's Dialogue (1632) compared Copernican theory with older models; in 1633 he was tried in Rome, found guilty of 'vehement suspicion of heresy', made to recite an abjuration, and kept under house arrest for the remaining nine years of his life.
c-galileo-1633.label: consensus

c-galileo-1992.text: On 31 October 1992 Pope John Paul II gave a much-misinterpreted speech on the Galileo affair; 'There was no re-trial or pardon'.
c-galileo-1992.label: consensus

c-kepler.text: Using Tycho Brahe's precise observations, Johannes Kepler, whom Tycho had invited to his court near Prague, found that Mars moves in an elliptical orbit; he published this in Astronomia Nova (1609), set out three laws of planetary motion, and completed the Rudolphine Tables (1627).
c-kepler.label: consensus

c-principia.text: Newton's Principia, published in 1687, set out his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation; Edmond Halley persuaded him to write it, during the years (1669-87) when Newton was Lucasian professor at Cambridge.
c-principia.label: consensus

c-shapin.text: Steven Shapin's The Scientific Revolution (1996) begins: 'There was no such thing as the Scientific Revolution, and this is a book about it'; he describes instead 'a diverse array of cultural practices aimed at understanding explaining, and controlling the natural world'.
c-shapin.label: debated
c-shapin.note: Shapin does not deny that natural knowledge changed; he denies that the change was one coherent event. H. Floris Cohen (2010) defends a rebuilt version of the concept.

c-cohen.text: H. Floris Cohen (2010) keeps the idea of a 17th-century Scientific Revolution but rebuilds it as 'six distinct, yet tightly interconnected revolutionary transformations', and asks why modern science emerged in Europe 'rather than in Greece, China, or the Islamic world'.
c-cohen.label: debated
c-cohen.note: From the book's catalogue description. Cohen's approach is comparative; Shapin's stresses variety within Europe.

c-print-debate.text: Elizabeth Eisenstein (1979) held that printed books enabled a stable and fixed culture of learning; Adrian Johns (1998) argues that 'a multiplicity of competing and idiosyncratic cultures of print' emerged, undermined by 'rampant and labyrinthine practices of book piracy'.
c-print-debate.label: debated
c-print-debate.note: Both positions as summarised by Kirkus Reviews; Eisenstein's own book was not consulted. Johns accepts that printed books 'stabilized texts and led to a degree of fixity in available knowledge'.

c-ulughbeg.text: Ulugh Beg's observatory was established at Samarkand in the 1420s; his zij, and especially his star catalogue of 1,018 stars, became 'the standard, in wide use throughout the Islamic world', and Thomas Hyde published a Latin translation of the catalogue in 1665.
c-ulughbeg.label: approx
c-ulughbeg.note: The date is uncertain: the University of Michigan page gives 1420, while Britannica says the observatory was 'begun in 1428'.

c-jantar.text: The Jantar Mantar at Jaipur, built in the early 18th century through the impetus of the prince Jai Singh II, is a set of some twenty main fixed instruments designed for observing astronomical positions with the naked eye, part of a tradition of Ptolemaic positional astronomy shared by many civilizations.
c-jantar.label: consensus

c-milrev-roberts.text: The phrase 'military revolution' appeared, little noticed, in 1956; in the view associated with Michael Roberts, complex and costly gunpowder technology forced states to become more efficient.
c-milrev-roberts.label: debated
c-milrev-roberts.note: As summarised by Encyclopaedia Universalis. For the critics, see Black, Hall and Lynn below.

c-milrev-parker.text: Geoffrey Parker's The Military Revolution (1988) revived the debate; as the Christian Science Monitor's review puts it, the military revolution 'marks the 16th century no less than the Renaissance and the Reformation'.
c-milrev-parker.label: debated
c-milrev-parker.note: Parker's thesis drew criticism from several directions; see Black, Hall and Lynn.

c-milrev-critics.text: Jeremy Black argued that the decisive technical advances came only in the second half of the 17th century and that the revolution of the state came first; Bert Hall found that artillery was adopted slowly and long of uncertain effect; John Lynn, studying the French army, found its earlier growth out of proportion to the monarchy's rudimentary administrative and fiscal framework, with the real take-off coming later.
c-milrev-critics.label: debated
c-milrev-critics.note: As summarised by Encyclopaedia Universalis, which notes that not everyone agrees on what belongs under the label.

c-voc-shares.text: The Dutch East India Company (VOC), launched in 1602, 'introduced easily transferable shares, and within days buyers had begun to trade them'; Lodewijk Petram writes that its launch 'initiated Amsterdam's transformation'.
c-voc-shares.label: consensus

c-voc-company.text: The VOC held a monopoly of Dutch trade from the Cape of Good Hope to the Strait of Magellan, renamed Jacatra (now Jakarta) Batavia in 1619 and was dissolved in 1799.
c-voc-company.label: consensus

c-spinoza-herem.text: On 27 July 1656 Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community issued Baruch Spinoza 'the harshest writ of herem' (ban), and 'it was never rescinded'.
c-spinoza-herem.label: consensus

c-spinoza-why.text: Why Spinoza was banned is uncertain: Steven Nadler writes, 'We do not know for certain what Spinoza's "monstrous deeds" and "abominable heresies" were alleged to have been'.
c-spinoza-why.label: debated
c-spinoza-why.note: Nadler's own suggestion is that they were the ideas Spinoza later published: that the soul is not immortal, that there is no providential God, and that the Law is not literally of divine origin or still binding.

c-civilwars.text: The English Civil Wars ran from 1642 to 1651; in Ireland, rebels sought to restore the Roman Catholic Church to its pre-Reformation position.
c-civilwars.label: consensus

c-glorious.text: In the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 the Catholic James II was replaced by Mary II and William III, prince of Orange and stadholder of the Netherlands.
c-glorious.label: consensus

c-boe-1694.text: The Bank of England was 'founded as a private bank in 1694 to act as banker to the Government', primarily to fund the war against France; William and Mary were two of its original stockholders.
c-boe-1694.label: consensus

c-nw1989.text: Douglass North and Barry Weingast (1989) argued that the institutions created after the Glorious Revolution served the winners' goals of secure property rights and an end to confiscatory government: 'the new institutions allowed the government to commit credibly to upholding property rights', as 'the evidence from capital markets shows'.
c-nw1989.label: debated
c-nw1989.note: A very influential argument in economics; Gary Cox (2012) and Steven Pincus and James Robinson question its scope and mechanism.

c-cox2012.text: Gary Cox (2012) finds that the evidence 'supports a view of the Revolution as a watershed', but argues it 'should have affected a narrower range of transactions than North and Weingast envisioned', working through Parliament's power to grant taxes for limited periods, its ability to block new government debt, and ministerial responsibility; 'Domestic property rights enforcement was thus little affected by the Revolution'.
c-cox2012.label: debated
c-cox2012.note: Cox keeps the idea that the Revolution changed what the Crown could credibly promise, but narrows where it mattered.

c-pincus-robinson.text: Steven Pincus and James Robinson argue that 'the Revolution Settlement actually established very few new de jure rules or rights', and that 'Rather than being de jure, the most significant of these were de facto'.
c-pincus-robinson.label: debated
c-pincus-robinson.note: Written for Douglass North's 90th birthday; they accept that the Revolution brought significant changes but locate them in de facto practice rather than in new formal rules.

c-santafe.text: Pedro de Peralta founded Santa Fe as the new capital of New Mexico in 1610; the Palace of the Governors there was erected about the same time.
c-santafe.label: consensus

c-pueblo-revolt.text: Spanish missionaries burned the Pueblos' ceremonial pits (kivas), masks and other sacred objects; on 10 August 1680 Popé led a full-scale revolt, and the Spaniards, who took refuge in the Palace of the Governors, fled New Mexico, leaving 400 dead, including 21 priests.
c-pueblo-revolt.label: approx
c-pueblo-revolt.note: The death toll is Britannica's figure.

c-pueblo-1692.text: The Pueblos remained free until 1692, when Diego de Vargas began the Spanish reconquest of New Mexico; by the end of 1692 most Pueblos 'had been restored to the Spanish empire without a shot being fired', but Santa Fe had to be recaptured by force in December 1693.
c-pueblo-1692.label: consensus
c-pueblo-1692.note: Britannica says New Mexico 'was reconquered' in 1692; Torrez separates the peaceful entry of 1692 from 1693, when 'Santa Fe was recaptured after a fierce battle that lasted two days.'

c-quebec.text: Samuel de Champlain began the settlement of Quebec in 1608; in New France the fur trade remained the chief concern of everyone except the missionaries.
c-quebec.label: consensus

c-haudenosaunee.text: The Haudenosaunee ('the people of the longhouse') formed a confederacy of five nations that became known to the English as the Six Nations after the Tuscarora joined in 1722.
c-haudenosaunee.label: consensus

c-league-date.text: When the Haudenosaunee League was founded is disputed: Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields argued from a solar eclipse that it was founded on 31 August 1142, but David Henige (1999) finds 'no serious evidence' for this; other proposed dates vary widely, among them about 1400-1450 (Lewis Henry Morgan) and about 1600 (W. M. Beauchamp: 'the year 1600 will do').
c-league-date.label: debated
c-league-date.note: Henige lists a sampling of eighteen proposed dates. He allows that no one can rule out 1142, but argues that the founding story probably began to evolve around the turn of the 19th century.

c-jamestown.text: On 13 May 1607 English colonists chose Jamestown, 'the first permanent English settlement in North America'; the winter of 1609-10 became known as the 'Starving Time', and on 30 July 1619 Governor Yeardley called the first representative legislative assembly.
c-jamestown.label: consensus

c-1619-arrival.text: In 1619 'the 20 and odd Africans' who reached Virginia were captives taken by the English warship White Lion from the Portuguese slave ship San Juan Bautista.
c-1619-arrival.label: consensus

c-virginia-law.text: Slavery was recognized in Virginia's statutory law in 1662, and its slave laws were codified in 1705.
c-virginia-law.label: consensus

c-1619-debate.text: In December 2019 the historians Gordon Wood, James McPherson, Sean Wilentz, James Oakes and Victoria Bynum asked the New York Times to correct its 1619 Project, calling 'not true' its claim that protecting slavery was a main reason for the American Revolution; Times Magazine editor Jake Silverstein 'defended the claims in the project's lead essay', and Nikole Hannah-Jones told the Daily Princetonian, 'We don't agree that the areas that they are disputing need to be corrected.' In March 2020 the Times changed the passage; Silverstein said it now made clear 'that this was a primary motivation for some of the colonists'.
c-1619-debate.label: debated
c-1619-debate.note: Adam Serwer argues that the fight is less about facts than about national identity.

c-plymouth.text: At Plymouth, founded in 1620, half the passengers and crew of the Mayflower died of disease and malnutrition between December 1620 and March 1621; a treaty with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, signed on 22 March 1621, was honoured by both sides until after his death in 1661.
c-plymouth.label: consensus

c-kpw.text: King Philip's War (June 1675 to August 1676), which pitted Native Americans against English settlers and their Indian allies and takes its name from Massasoit's son Metacom, whom the English called Philip, was 'one of the bloodiest conflicts (per capita) in U.S. history'.
c-kpw.label: consensus

c-kpw-toll.text: Some 800 English men, women and children died in King Philip's War, and one-third of New England's approximately 100 English towns were burned and abandoned; among Native people, 2,000 died of battle wounds, 3,000 of disease or starvation, and 1,000 were sold into slavery.
c-kpw-toll.label: approx
c-kpw-toll.note: Figures from Ian Aldrich in Yankee magazine (2007), a popular source; treat them as rough orders of size.

pages.title: The world joined
pages.lede: Between 1488 and 1498 Portuguese and Spanish voyages reached the Cape of Good Hope, the Caribbean and India, and within a few decades Spaniards had taken the Mexica capital and seized the Inca ruler. This chapter follows what came of those encounters down to about 1750, and the evidence, from Nahua testimony to Antarctic ice, by which we know it.
body: In December 1488 Bartolomeu Dias returned to Portugal having rounded the Cape of Good Hope without seeing it. [[c-dias-1488]] On 12 October 1492 Columbus's ships sighted land across the Atlantic. [[c-columbus-1492-voyage]] In 1494 Spain and Portugal agreed at Tordesillas on a line in the Atlantic dividing their claims, [[c-tordesillas-1494]] and on 20 May 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut by sea. [[c-dagama-1498]]

Within a few decades Spaniards had taken Tenochtitlan, in 1521, [[c-tenochtitlan-fall-1521]] seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca, in 1532, [[c-cajamarca-1532]] and found silver at Potosí. [[c-potosi-silver-mita]] The pages that follow take the story on: the Great Dying and the exchange of plants and animals (13.5), silver and world trade (13.6), the Atlantic slave trade (13.7), the Reformation and Habsburg Spain (13.8, 13.9), the Islamic empires and East Asia (13.10, 13.11), science (13.12), money and war in Europe (13.13) and North America (13.14).

The evidence comes from many sides. The Mexica account of the conquest survives in Book 12 of the Florentine Codex, written in Nahuatl and Spanish under the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and completed in 1575-77. [[c-florentine-codex]] [[c-florentine-book12]] Guaman Poma's illustrated Andean chronicle, with a prologue to King Philip III, is a critical account of Spanish rule in Peru. [[c-guamanpoma-chronicle]]

Numbers come from colonial records and modern science. Colonial counts let Livi Bacci trace the collapse of Hispaniola's people, [[c-hispaniola-collapse]] while ancient DNA suggests that older estimates of the Caribbean's population were too high. [[c-taino-pop-estimates]] The records of 34,948 voyages underlie the estimate that some 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard slave ships. [[c-slavevoyages-125m]] And Lewis and Maslin have proposed that a dip in carbon dioxide in Antarctic ice, centred on 1610, records the deaths of about 50 million Indigenous Americans and the regrowth of forests that followed. [[c-orbis-spike]]

practice.q: Why do Lewis and Maslin link a dip in carbon dioxide in Antarctic ice, centred on 1610, to the European arrival in the Americas?
choices: Mass deaths led to forest regrowth, which absorbed carbon dioxide
Ships' logs show the dip began with Columbus's crossing of 1492
Smoke from the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 reached Antarctica
Silver smelting at Potosí after the 1540s released carbon dioxide
practice.why: They tie the deaths of about 50 million Indigenous Americans to the regrowth of forests, which drew carbon dioxide out of the air; they call the dip the 'Orbis Spike'.

wrong.1: The dip is measured in ice cores, and it is centred on 1610, more than a century after the 1492 crossing.
wrong.2: The signal is a fall in carbon dioxide, which they tie to forest regrowth, not smoke.
wrong.3: Their explanation is regrowth after mass deaths, not mining; Potosí's silver was found in 1542-45.

practice.q: How should a reader understand the figure of 'some 12.5 million' Africans forced aboard slave ships?
choices: As an estimate built up from the records of 34,948 voyages
As an exact head count taken from African port registers
As the number who survived the crossing and landed alive
As a total the Portuguese crown recorded in its tax rolls
practice.why: The NEH describes the SlaveVoyages database as reflecting 34,948 voyages; the total is an estimate built on them.

wrong.1: The figure is an estimate from voyage records, not a count of named individuals.
wrong.2: It counts those forced aboard ships; arrivals are discussed on 13.7.
wrong.3: The figure is an estimate built from the voyage records of the SlaveVoyages database, not a royal record.

pages.title: Portugal's road to Asia
pages.lede: Between 1488 and 1511 Portuguese fleets rounded Africa, reached India by sea, touched Brazil and seized Goa and Melaka. A treaty with Spain in 1494 had already divided the two kingdoms' claims along a line in the Atlantic.
body: Portugal's voyages down the African coast (12.6) led on to India. Bartolomeu Dias, who probably sailed in August 1487, rounded the Cape of Good Hope without seeing it and was home in December 1488. [[c-dias-1488]] Who named the cape is uncertain: Barros says Dias called it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it, while Duarte Pacheco credits the name to Dias himself. [[c-cape-name-dispute]] In June 1494 Spain and Portugal agreed at Tordesillas to divide their claims along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, well beyond the pope's earlier line at 100 leagues; what lay east went to Portugal, what lay west to Spain. [[c-tordesillas-1494]]

Vasco da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 and rounded the Cape that November. At Malindi he took on a Gujarati pilot who knew the route, and he reached Calicut (12.10) on 20 May 1498. [[c-dagama-1498]] The meeting went badly: in Britannica's words, the Zamorin's goodwill 'was dispelled by da Gama's insignificant gifts and rude behaviour.' [[c-dagama-calicut-gifts]] Only 55 of his 170 men survived the voyage; he reached Lisbon in September 1499. [[c-dagama-losses]]
In 1500 a fleet under Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted Brazil on 22 April, took formal possession, and sailed on to Calicut; Dias, sailing with it, was lost at sea near the Cape. [[c-cabral-brazil-1500]]

Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa by assault in November 1510, putting its Muslim defenders to the sword, and Melaka (12.10) in July 1511. [[c-albuquerque-goa-melaka]] His aim was permanent fortresses with settled populations, though his first plan for a fort at Hormuz, in 1507, had to be dropped because of differences with his captains; in 1515 he returned and gained control of part of the island. [[c-albuquerque-fortresses]] Goa became the capital of the Portuguese Indies; UNESCO, calling it 'the former capital of the Portuguese Indies', says that its churches, one of which holds the tomb of Francis Xavier, 'illustrate the evangelization of Asia'. [[c-goa-unesco-churches]]

Event

practice.q: What did the Treaty of Tordesillas change compared with the pope's earlier line?
choices: It moved the line from 100 to 370 leagues west of Cape Verde
It divided the world between Portugal and the Ottoman empire
It answered Cabral's landing in Brazil in 1500 by moving the line
It moved the line so that lands to its west went to Portugal
practice.why: The treaty set the line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, against the pope's 100; since Portugal took what lay east of it, moving the line west enlarged Portugal's share.

wrong.1: It was an agreement between Spain and Portugal.
wrong.2: It was made in 1494; Cabral sighted Brazil in 1500.
wrong.3: Lands to the west of the line went to Spain, those to the east to Portugal.

practice.q: Which description best fits Albuquerque's strategy in Asia?
choices: Holding fortified ports with settled populations, like Goa
Winning over the Zamorin of Calicut with gifts and trade treaties
Settling farmers along the coast of Brazil after Cabral's landing
Governing Goa through an alliance with its Muslim defenders
practice.why: Britannica says he aimed at permanent fortresses with settled populations, and he took Goa and Melaka by force.

wrong.1: At Calicut it was da Gama whose gifts dispelled the Zamorin's goodwill; Albuquerque took ports by force.
wrong.2: Brazil was claimed by Cabral in 1500; Albuquerque's conquests were Goa and Melaka.
wrong.3: When he took Goa, its Muslim defenders were put to the sword.

pages.title: Columbus and the Caribbean
pages.lede: Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492 and never gave up the belief that he had reached Asia. On Hispaniola the Taíno population collapsed within a generation, mostly before smallpox arrived. The friar Antonio de Montesinos and Bartolomé de las Casas challenged the colonists, and laws to restrain them had limited effect.
body: Columbus's fleet sailed on 3 August 1492, and on 12 October land was sighted from the Pinta. [[c-columbus-1492-voyage]] Where he first landed, the island called Guanahani, is hotly disputed, though San Salvador in the Bahamas is generally preferred. [[c-guanahani-landfall]] He convinced himself that Cuba was the Asian mainland and never gave up the belief that he had reached Asia. [[c-columbus-asia-belief]] His aims included religious ones: his Book of Prophecies, compiled after 1500, presents the voyages, in its modern publisher's words, as 'a first step toward the liberation of Jerusalem'. [[c-columbus-prophecies]] Carol Delaney argues that he wanted gold to launch a crusade, a reading one reviewer found thinly evidenced. [[c-columbus-delaney]]

When the Santa María ran aground on 25 December 1492, Columbus built a fort, La Navidad, on Hispaniola with help from the Taíno chief Guacanagarí and left 39 men there. [[c-navidad-1492]] The Taíno were an Arawakan-speaking people of the Greater Antilles. [[c-taino-people]] How many there were is disputed. Britannica says they may have numbered one or two million; Livi Bacci estimates 200,000-300,000 for Hispaniola; and a 2021 ancient-DNA study concludes that estimates of hundreds of thousands across the Caribbean are too large. [[c-taino-pop-estimates]]

Whatever the starting figure, the fall was steep. On Livi Bacci's figures 60,000 people remained in 1508 and just over 26,000 in 1514, and after the smallpox of 1518-19 only a few thousand. [[c-hispaniola-collapse]] Because the Taíno were near extinction before smallpox struck, he argues that conquest itself explains the collapse: gold mining, the encomienda, displacement and falling fertility. [[c-livibacci-causes]] On the fourth Sunday of Advent 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached against the colonists, asking, 'Are they not men? Do they not have rational souls?' [[c-montesinos-1511]] The Laws of Burgos of December 1512 required encomenderos to feed, clothe and instruct the Indians and banned whipping, but in practice they did not improve conditions. [[c-burgos-1512]]

Bartolomé de las Casas, who had sailed to the New World in 1502 and was later ordained a priest (accounts of the date range from 1507 to 1513), became the colonists' leading critic. [[c-lascasas-career]] The New Laws of 1542-43 banned the enslavement of Indians and stopped encomiendas passing to heirs; a revolt followed in Peru, in which the first viceroy was beheaded, and the ban on inheritance was repealed in 1545-46. [[c-new-laws-1542]] At Valladolid in 1550-51 Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda debated whether Aristotle's idea of natural slavery applied to the Indians. [[c-valladolid-1550]] A 2023 thesis argues that Spaniards then read the idea broadly, as an inferiority that education and faith could overcome. [[c-fuxa-natural-slavery]] His writings, among them A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552), became a major source of the 'Black Legend' of exceptional Spanish cruelty, and Spanish patriots condemned him for it. Critics say he exaggerated, though modern scholarship has largely supported his toll of Native deaths, while blaming most of them on disease rather than cruelty; and, one historian writes, whether or not he exaggerated, the Brief Account 'remains one of the most important documents ever written on human rights'. [[c-lascasas-blacklegend]]

pages.title: The conquest of Mexico
pages.lede: Between 1519 and 1521 Hernán Cortés, with a small Spanish force and Tlaxcalan allies, took Tenochtitlan as smallpox struck the city. Mexica memories written down in Nahuatl, and historians such as Matthew Restall, put Indigenous people at the centre of the story.
body: Hernán Cortés landed at Tabasco in March 1519, founded Veracruz and sank his ships. [[c-cortes-1519]] Malintzin, also called Doña Marina, became his interpreter and mistress and bore him a son. [[c-malintzin-marina]] Tlaxcala first fought him and then became his most faithful ally, and on 8 November 1519 he entered Tenochtitlan, the Mexica capital (12.11), with his small Spanish force and about 1,000 Tlaxcaltecs. [[c-tlaxcala-ally]]

Cortés soon seized Moctezuma, who died around 30 June 1520. [[c-moctezuma-seized]] In September or October 1520 smallpox reached Tenochtitlan. It killed Moctezuma's successor, and by one estimate a third to a half of the population died during the epidemic. [[c-smallpox-tenochtitlan]] The capture of the city was completed on 13 August 1521. [[c-tenochtitlan-fall-1521]]

The Mexica side of the story survives in Book 12 of the Florentine Codex, with chapters on the massacre at Cholula, Moctezuma's meeting with Cortés and the plague. [[c-florentine-book12]] It was set down in Nahuatl and Spanish under the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and completed in 1575-77, more than 50 years after the events. [[c-florentine-codex]]

The older, heroic story gave the decisive role to the Spaniards. Matthew Restall calls this a myth: the conquest, he argues, 'relied heavily on black and native allies', and Indigenous people saw it 'as a native civil war in which the Spaniards played an important but secondary role.' [[c-restall-myths]]

pages.title: The Inca and Spanish America
pages.lede: Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532, as the empire emerged from civil war, and within three years Spaniards held Cuzco and had founded Lima. The silver of Potosí was mined with forced labour whose long-run effects are still measured, and in Mexico the devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe grew from a tradition whose early history is debated.
body: The Inca empire (12.11) was divided against itself. After Huayna Capac died, his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fought a civil war, by one account for seven years, and Atahualpa had won by 1532, just as Pizarro arrived. [[c-inca-civilwar]] At Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 Pizarro's force of about 168 men seized Atahualpa. [[c-cajamarca-1532]] Atahualpa filled the room where he was held with gold and silver as ransom, but he was strangled in 1533; Britannica gives the date as 29 August, World History Encyclopedia as 26 July. [[c-atahualpa-ransom-death]] Cuzco was occupied without a struggle in November 1533, and Pizarro founded Lima in 1535; he was killed by Almagro's former supporters in 1541. [[c-cuzco-lima]]

Between 1542 and 1545 silver was found at the Cerro Rico of Potosí, which UNESCO calls 'reputed to be the world's largest industrial complex in the 16th century'; workers were forced into its mines under the mita, a system of mandatory labour. [[c-potosi-silver-mita]] Its silver's place in world trade is the subject of 13.6. The mining mita lasted from 1573 to 1812, and Melissa Dell has found that districts once subject to it today have household consumption about 25 percent lower, and child stunting about 6 percentage points higher, than districts just outside its old boundary. [[c-dell-mita-effects]]

Andean voices survive. Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's illustrated Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (1612-15), a critical account of Spanish rule in Peru, includes a prologue addressed to King Philip III. [[c-guamanpoma-chronicle]] In Mexico, Catholic tradition holds that in December 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin at Tepeyac, and that her image appeared on his tilma before Bishop Zumárraga. [[c-guadalupe-tradition]] In 2002 John Paul II canonized Juan Diego, praising him for 'accepting the Christian message without forgoing his indigenous identity'. [[c-juandiego-canonized]]

The written record begins later, with Miguel Sánchez's account in 1648 and Luis Laso de la Vega's in Nahuatl in 1649. Stafford Poole judges that the story's symbolism 'does not rest on any objective historical basis', while those who uphold the tradition argue, or presume, that Sánchez drew on oral testimony or on an earlier unpublished account. [[c-guadalupe-written-record]] Sánchez himself identified Tepeyac as a pre-Christian pilgrimage site of the goddess Tonantzin, whose place he believed Guadalupe had providentially taken, while Sahagún opposed the devotion as a thinly veiled continuation of Indigenous religion. [[c-guadalupe-tonantzin]]
