pages.title: The Great Dying and the Columbian exchange
pages.lede: After 1492 the Indigenous population of the Americas collapsed; one study puts the loss at 90 percent within a century. Historians still argue over how much was due to new diseases and how much to slavery, overwork and famine. Crops and animals crossed the ocean too, and some scientists think the die-off left a mark in the atmosphere.
body: Chapter 12 set out the estimates of how many people lived in the Americas in 1492 (12.11); a 2019 synthesis by Koch and colleagues gives 60.5 million. [[c-gd-pop1492]] The same team estimates that European epidemics removed 90 percent of them within a century, a 'Great Dying'. [[c-gd-loss90]] Britannica gives a range of 50 to 95 percent by 1650 across the Americas, and more than 99 percent on most Caribbean islands (13.2). [[c-gd-brit-range]] Measles, smallpox, influenza, mumps, typhus and whooping cough were all new to the Americas. [[c-gd-diseases]]

Was disease the whole story? Andrés Reséndez argues that slavery, overwork and famine also killed, and estimates that 2.5 to 5 million Native Americans were enslaved between Columbus's time and 1900. [[c-gd-resendez]] A 2026 study points out that no colonial-era mass grave has yet been shown to hold victims of smallpox, and proposes criteria for finding them. [[c-gd-burials]] Ancient DNA can help: ten of 24 people sampled from a cemetery of the cocoliztli epidemic of 1545-50 at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, in Oaxaca, carried a Salmonella bacterium, a possible cause of that outbreak. [[c-gd-cocoliztli]]

Alfred Crosby named the traffic between the hemispheres 'the Columbian Exchange' in 1972. [[c-gd-crosby]] Maize, potatoes, cassava and sweet potatoes went to the Old World, where maize changed farming most, in Asia, Europe and Africa; cassava reached Africa in the 16th century. [[c-gd-crops]] In the other direction, cattle and horses ran wild and multiplied on the Pampas and the Great Plains. [[c-gd-livestock]]

The die-off may even show in the air. Lewis and Maslin proposed in 2015 that a dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide around 1610, which they called the 'Orbis Spike', marks the start of the Anthropocene. [[c-gd-orbis]] Koch and colleagues calculate that regrowth on abandoned land in the Americas took up the equivalent of 3.5 parts per million of CO2 directly, and that with carbon-cycle feedbacks and land-use change elsewhere the extra uptake came to about 5 ppm, 47-67 percent of an observed fall of 7-10 ppm. On their figures the fall cannot be explained without the regrowth, though the regrowth does not explain all of it. [[c-gd-regrowth]] Geologists have not adopted an Anthropocene epoch: in 2024 they decisively rejected a proposal that would have started it in the mid-20th century. [[c-anthropocene-2024]]

pages.title: Silver and the first global economy
pages.lede: Spanish America's silver went east to Europe and west across the Pacific to China. Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez date the birth of global trade to the founding of Manila in 1571; others place it in the 19th century. Scholars also still debate how far American silver drove prices up in 16th-century Spain.
body: At Potosí, in the Andes, silver was found between 1542 and 1545, and in the 16th century the site was regarded as the world's largest industrial complex (13.4). [[c-ag-potosi]] In New Spain, Zacatecas was founded in 1546 after a rich silver lode was found. [[c-ag-zacatecas]] By one estimate Spanish America produced about 150,000 tons of silver between 1500 and 1800, perhaps 80 percent of the world's output. [[c-ag-150k]]

Part of it went west, across the Pacific. Flynn and Giráldez argue that global trade began with the founding of Manila in 1571, and that silver flowed to China because it was worth twice as much there as in the rest of the world. [[c-ag-flynn]] Peter Coclanis, following Flynn and Giráldez, puts the galleons' cargo from Acapulco in the 17th century at an average of about two million pesos a year, more than fifty tons; Manila was little more than a way station for silver on its way to China. [[c-ag-galleon]] In 1581 the Ming promulgated throughout the empire the 'single whip', which turned land tax and labour service into one payment in silver; Britannica calls it 'little more than a bookkeeping change at best', while EBSCO's summary stresses that it depended on foreign silver. [[c-ag-singlewhip]] Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson use a different test, converging commodity prices. By that test they find no sign that the world economy was integrated by 1492 or 1498, and 'a very big globalization bang' in the 19th century, a much later start than Flynn and Giráldez propose. [[c-ag-orourke]]

Did silver also drive up prices in Europe? In 1556 Martín de Azpilcueta, of the School of Salamanca, set out an early version of the quantity theory of money. [[c-ag-navarrus]] In 1934 Earl Hamilton argued that American treasure was the principal cause of Spain's price revolution; John Munro notes that prices were already rising in 1516-20, before large silver imports. [[c-ag-hamilton]] Isotopes in coins point both ways. In one study, Anne-Marie Desaulty and colleagues found that Mexican silver did not enter Spanish coinage before the early 17th century, which Desaulty said calls into question the link between American metal and the price revolution. In another, they found Mexican silver in English coins from the mid-1550s, though Potosí's appeared only nearly a century later, and Science News reported that this study adds 'hard data' to theories linking American silver to inflation. [[c-ag-isotopes]]

pages.title: The Atlantic slave trade
pages.lede: Between the 16th and the 19th centuries about 12.5 million Africans were shipped to the Americas, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing. Most were taken to the Caribbean and Brazil. African rulers responded to the trade in different ways, and economists still debate its long-term effects on Africa.
body: The SlaveVoyages database estimates that about 12.5 million Africans were shipped to the Americas and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage; Britannica gives a lower total of 10 to 12 million. [[c-st-total]] Many died before the ships sailed: an estimated 10 to 15 percent of captives died on the way to the coast. [[c-st-coast]] The trade grew over time: about 278,000 people were embarked in the 16th century and about 6.5 million in the 18th, more than half of the total. [[c-st-century]]

Demand for enslaved labour rose sharply with the growth of sugar plantations in the Caribbean, [[c-st-sugar]] which received about 52 percent of those landed; Brazil took about 39 percent, and North America under 4 percent (about 388,000 people, on Gates's figures). [[c-st-dest]] Spain supplied its American colonies through asientos, monopoly contracts granted by the crown; the last went to Britain's South Sea Company in 1713, for 4,800 slaves a year for 30 years. [[c-st-asiento]]

African rulers responded in different ways. In 1526 Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo (12.8), protested to João III of Portugal that 'our country is being completely depopulated'. [[c-st-afonso]] Two centuries later Agaja of Dahomey conquered Allada and the coastal state of Ouidah, and in time accepted the trade, on condition that it be a royal monopoly. [[c-st-agaja]] Economists still argue over the long-term cost: Nathan Nunn finds that the countries from which the most slaves were taken are poorer today, while Margherita Bottero and Björn Wallace reply that the relationship 'did not become significantly negative until 1970'. [[c-st-nunn]]

pages.title: The Reformation
pages.lede: Within a quarter-century of Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517, Anabaptist and Reformed churches had formed and Henry VIII had made himself head of the Church of England. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent. Settlements at Augsburg in 1555 and Westphalia in 1648 followed, and historians still debate how religious the Thirty Years' War was and what Westphalia founded.
body: On 31 October 1517, by the traditional account, Martin Luther posted 95 Theses at the castle church in Wittenberg. [[c-ref-theses]] Whether he nailed them to the door is debated: the historian Erwin Iserloh argued in 1961 that he never did, though it is certain that Luther sent them to Archbishop Albrecht. [[c-ref-nailing]] Print may have helped: Jared Rubin finds that cities with a press by 1500 (12.5) were at least 29 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600. [[c-ref-print]] In 1543, in On the Jews and Their Lies, Luther urged that synagogues be set on fire; in 1994 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America rejected 'this violent invective'. [[c-ref-jews]] Eric Gritsch judged that Luther's arguments against Jews were 'theological, not biological', though he notes that the National Socialists used Luther to support their racist antisemitism, and the ELCA deplores 'the appropriation of Luther's words by modern anti-Semites'. [[c-ref-gritsch]]

Reform soon took many forms. In January 1525, at Felix Manz's house in Zurich, radicals who had broken with Ulrich Zwingli baptized each other, the start of the Anabaptist movement; [[c-ref-anabaptists]] in Geneva, John Calvin's Ecclesiastical Ordinances of 1541 organised a Reformed church; [[c-ref-calvin]] in England, the Act of Supremacy of 1534 made Henry VIII supreme head of the Church of England. [[c-ref-supremacy]] Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540, [[c-ref-jesuits]] and the Council of Trent (1545-63) defined virtually every doctrine Protestants contested. [[c-ref-trent]]

The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each ruler in the Empire choose Catholicism or Lutheranism for his lands, but made no provision for Calvinists. [[c-ref-augsburg]] The Thirty Years' War killed, by Peter Wilson's estimate, about 1.8 million soldiers and at least 3.2 million civilians, cutting the Empire's population by at least a fifth, [[c-ref-30yw]] though Wilson denies that it was a religious conflict. [[c-ref-wilson-religion]] The Peace of Westphalia (1648) extended toleration to Calvinists and confirmed the Dutch and Swiss republics as independent. [[c-ref-westphalia]] Whether it founded a modern system of sovereign states is disputed: Andreas Osiander calls that picture 'a past that is largely imaginary'. [[c-ref-sovereignty]]

pages.title: Habsburg Spain
pages.lede: Philip II governed his empire from his desk in Spain, yet his state was declared bankrupt in 1557 and he stopped paying his lenders four times. In 1588 only about 65 of the Armada's 130 to 150 ships returned to Spain, and in 1609-14 some 300,000 Moriscos were expelled. Historians still debate whether, and how, Spain then 'declined'.
body: In 1555 Philip II took over his father's dominions. He made Madrid his capital, built the Escorial as his residence and the centre of his empire, and ruled from his desk. [[c-hs-philip]] In 1557 the state was declared bankrupt, and not for the last time. [[c-hs-1557]] Yet the bankers kept lending. Philip stopped all payments to his lenders four times, and Mauricio Drelichman and Hans-Joachim Voth argue that a 'cheat the cheater' mechanism kept the lending going and profitable overall. [[c-hs-dv]]

In 1588 Philip sent the Armada against England: some 130 to 150 ships and 18,000 men. After an English fireship attack off Calais and the fiercest fighting of the campaign at Gravelines, only about 65 ships made it back to Spain; Medina Sidonia himself reached Santander. [[c-hs-armada]] Between 1609 and 1614 about 300,000 Moriscos, converts from Islam, were expelled from Spain (on 1492, see 12.6), some 120,000 of them from Valencia; most settled in North Africa and Constantinople. [[c-hs-moriscos]]

Teresa of Ávila (1515-82) originated the Carmelite Reform; canonised in 1622, she became in 1970 the first woman named a Doctor of the Church. [[c-hs-teresa]] Miguel de Cervantes, Alcalá de Henares's 'great son', published Don Quixote in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. [[c-hs-quixote]]

Was this the start of a decline? Contemporaries already wrote tracts asking why Spanish power had diminished. [[c-hs-contemp]] J. H. Elliott's 1961 essay 'The Decline of Spain' remains one of the best introductions to the question, and his work examined how Spain's leaders tried to avert decline; [[c-hs-elliott]] Henry Kamen argues that 19th- and 20th-century politicians and historians built 'a fictitious image' of 16th-century Spain, and examines 'the persistent obsession with the notion of national decline'. [[c-hs-kamen]]

pages.title: Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals
pages.lede: The Ottomans twice besieged Vienna, the Safavids made Shi'ism the religion of their state, and in India the Mughal emperor Akbar abolished a tax on non-Muslims, while Aurangzeb later reimposed the jizya. Historians still argue over the label 'gunpowder empires' that was given to all three.
body: Süleyman, known in Turkish as Kanuni, 'the Lawgiver', ruled from 1520 to 1566 [[c-suleyman-reign]] (on the Ottoman rise, see 12.7). In 1529 he besieged Vienna, but the siege was lifted. [[c-vienna-1529]] A second Ottoman siege, in 1683, was broken by a relief army under Charles of Lorraine and the Polish king Jan III Sobieski, [[c-vienna-1683]] a defeat Britannica sees as the beginning of the end of Ottoman domination in eastern Europe. [[c-vienna-meaning]] At Smyrna (Izmir) in 1665, Jews acclaimed Sabbatai Zevi as the messiah; his movement spread as far as Amsterdam and London and threatened the authority of the rabbis. [[c-sabbatai-1665]] In 1666, at Adrianople, he converted to Islam. [[c-sabbatai-1666]]

In July 1501 Ismail was enthroned as shah, ruling at first only Azerbaijan, and proclaimed Shi'ism the religion of his state, enforcing its creed and prayers in the mosques; [[c-safavid-1501]] he had taken the city of Tabriz that year. [[c-ismail-tabriz]] In 1514 his Sunni rival, the Ottoman sultan Selim I, defeated him heavily at Chaldiran. [[c-chaldiran-1514]] Abbas I, who came to the throne in 1588, moved the capital to Isfahan and made it the centre of Safavid architecture; the city fell to Afghan invaders in 1722. [[c-abbas-isfahan]]

In India, Akbar (r. 1556-1605) made marriage alliances with Rajput rulers and abolished the tax on pilgrims and the tax non-Muslims paid in place of military service. [[c-akbar-policy]] In 1575 work began on a hall for religious debate, the Ibadat Khana, at Fatehpur Sikri; at first only Muslim scholars debated there, but from 1578 Akbar brought Hindus, Parsis and Christians into the discussions. He never renounced Islam. [[c-akbar-debates]] Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. [[c-taj-mahal]] Under Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) the empire reached its greatest extent, but in 1679 he reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims, and Hindu temples were often destroyed. [[c-aurangzeb-rule]] Audrey Truschke argues that he acted for political rather than religious ends; a reviewer finds parts of her case debatable. [[c-aurangzeb-legacy]]

William McNeill and Marshall Hodgson called these states 'gunpowder empires'. [[c-gunpowder-term]] Recent historians answer that most of their armies still relied mainly on swords, spears and bows, and that their rulers' power may have rested more on governance. [[c-gunpowder-critics]] Gábor Ágoston stresses how pragmatically the Ottomans adapted firearms, but also points to intelligence, leadership and large, disciplined armies, [[c-agoston-firearms]] while Douglas Streusand keeps the label but treats the three empires as parts of one international system, and as complex polities in which Islam was one component among many. [[c-streusand]]

pages.title: East Asia
pages.lede: In 1644 a rebel army took Beijing and was driven out by Ming and Manchu troops; the Qing emperor Kangxi later sent troops to Taiwan and made a treaty with Russia. Catholic missionaries quarrelled over Chinese rites, Japan's Tokugawa shoguns banned Christianity, and a Japanese invasion in the 1590s killed at least 125,000 Koreans.
body: In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing with ease; a combined force of former Ming and Manchu troops then drove him out (on the Ming, see 12.9). [[c-li-1644]] The Manchus had founded their Qing dynasty in 1636, [[c-qing-1636]] and under Qing rule China's territory grew to three times its size and its population from some 150 million to 450 million. [[c-qing-growth]] Tree rings studied in 2024 show long megadroughts in northern China in 1576-93 and 1628-44, which the researchers argue contributed to the Ming collapse. [[c-ming-megadrought]]

The Kangxi emperor (r. 1661-1722) put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, begun by Wu Sangui, sent troops across the Taiwan Strait in 1683 and made the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia in 1689. [[c-kangxi-wars]] He also encouraged Western learning and Roman Catholicism. [[c-kangxi-catholic]] The Jesuit Matteo Ricci had reached Macau in 1582, taken to dressing as a Chinese scholar, and settled in Beijing in 1601. [[c-ricci]] The Jesuits held that Chinese ceremonies honouring Confucius and ancestors could be tolerated within limits; Dominicans and Franciscans disagreed and appealed to Rome, which banned the rites in 1704, 1715 and 1742 and allowed Catholics to join ceremonies for Confucius only in 1939. [[c-rites]]

In 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea as part of a plan to invade China through Korea, and his army took Seoul on 12 June. [[c-imjin-invasion]] Ming China sent armies to Korea's aid, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy hampered the Japanese at sea, and the invasion was abandoned after Hideyoshi died in 1598. [[c-imjin-war]] At least 125,000 Koreans died, and many Korean potters were carried off to Japan; relations were restored in 1607. [[c-imjin-cost]]

In Japan the Tokugawa shoguns governed from Edo from 1603 to 1867, a period of internal peace and economic growth. [[c-tokugawa]] Three decrees of the 1630s banned Christianity completely. [[c-exclusion-decrees]] Portuguese ships were excluded in 1639, and from 1641 the Dutch traded from Dejima, off Nagasaki, where Chinese merchants also came; relations with Korea, the Ryukyus and the Ainu ran through the domains of Tsushima, Satsuma and Matsumae. [[c-four-portals]] Historians long called this sakoku, the 'closed country', but Ronald Toby showed that the shogunate kept up an active network for gathering information abroad. [[c-toby-sakoku]] (On Christian missions elsewhere, see 13.8.)

pages.title: Science and the printed book
pages.lede: Between Copernicus's book of 1543 and Newton's Principia of 1687, astronomers put the Sun at the centre of the planets' motions, and the Church tried Galileo for defending the idea. Historians now argue over whether this was one 'Scientific Revolution' and over what printing did, while observatories at Samarkand and Jaipur belonged to other traditions.
body: The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed that the planets move around the Sun as a fixed point. His De revolutionibus was printed at Nuremberg in 1543, the year he died, [[c-copernicus]] with an unsigned letter by Andreas Osiander and a subtly altered title that made the book look less like a claim about the real world. [[c-osiander]] Tradition says Copernicus first saw the printed book on his deathbed. [[c-copernicus-deathbed]]

Working from Tycho Brahe's precise observations, Johannes Kepler found that Mars moves in an ellipse, published in Astronomia Nova (1609), and set out three laws of planetary motion. [[c-kepler]] In January 1610 Galileo found four moons circling Jupiter. [[c-galileo-moons]] In 1616 the Congregation of the Index declared false any theory that the Earth moved around the Sun and suspended Copernicus's book until it was corrected (the corrections followed in 1620). [[c-index-1616]] After Galileo's Dialogue (1632), he was tried in Rome, found guilty of 'vehement suspicion of heresy', made to abjure, and confined to his house for the rest of his life. [[c-galileo-1633]] In 1992 Pope John Paul II spoke about the affair, but there was no retrial or pardon. [[c-galileo-1992]]

Newton's Principia (1687), written at Edmond Halley's urging while Newton was a professor at Cambridge, set out three laws of motion and universal gravitation. [[c-principia]] Steven Shapin opens his history, 'There was no such thing as the Scientific Revolution, and this is a book about it', and sees instead a diverse array of practices; [[c-shapin]] H. Floris Cohen keeps the concept, rebuilt as six linked transformations, and asks why modern science arose in Europe rather than in Greece, China or the Islamic world. [[c-cohen]] Printing (12.5) is argued over too: Elizabeth Eisenstein held that books made learning stable and fixed, while Adrian Johns stresses competing cultures of print and rampant piracy. [[c-print-debate]]

Astronomers outside Europe worked in other traditions. Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand, built in the 1420s, produced a star catalogue that became the standard throughout the Islamic world and reached Latin in 1665. [[c-ulughbeg]] In the early 18th century Jai Singh II built the Jantar Mantar at Jaipur, about twenty fixed instruments for naked-eye observation in a tradition of Ptolemaic astronomy shared by many civilizations. [[c-jantar]]

pages.title: Money, states and war in Europe
pages.lede: Historians have long argued over how war, money and the state shaped one another in early modern Europe. Shares in the Dutch East India Company traded in Amsterdam from 1602, and England, after its civil wars and the Revolution of 1688-89, founded the Bank of England to pay for war with France. Whether that Revolution made the Crown's promises credible is still debated.
body: The phrase 'military revolution' appeared, little noticed, in 1956; in the view associated with Michael Roberts, costly gunpowder warfare forced states to become more efficient. [[c-milrev-roberts]] Geoffrey Parker revived the debate in 1988, arguing that the military revolution marks the 16th century as much as the Renaissance and the Reformation do. [[c-milrev-parker]] Critics questioned both the timing and the direction of cause: Jeremy Black placed the decisive changes in the later 17th century and argued that the state's own development came first; Bert Hall found that artillery spread slowly; and John Lynn found that France's army only really took off later. [[c-milrev-critics]]

The Dutch East India Company (VOC), launched in 1602, introduced shares that could be easily transferred, and buyers were trading them within days; Lodewijk Petram sees this as the start of Amsterdam's transformation. [[c-voc-shares]] The company held a monopoly of Dutch trade from the Cape of Good Hope to the Strait of Magellan, renamed Jacatra (now Jakarta) Batavia in 1619 and lasted until 1799. [[c-voc-company]] In the same city, in 1656, the Portuguese-Jewish community (on Iberia's Jews, see 12.6) placed Baruch Spinoza under its harshest ban, which was never lifted. [[c-spinoza-herem]] Its reasons are uncertain; Steven Nadler suspects the ideas Spinoza later published, such as his denial that the soul is immortal. [[c-spinoza-why]]

England's civil wars lasted from 1642 to 1651; in Ireland, rebels sought to restore the Catholic Church to its pre-Reformation position (on the Reformation, see 13.8). [[c-civilwars]] In the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 the Catholic James II was replaced by Mary II and William III, prince of Orange. [[c-glorious]] In 1694 the Bank of England was founded as a private bank to be the government's banker, chiefly to pay for the war against France; William and Mary were among its first stockholders. [[c-boe-1694]]

Douglass North and Barry Weingast (1989) argued that the new institutions after 1688 let the government commit credibly to upholding property rights, and pointed to evidence from capital markets. [[c-nw1989]] Gary Cox (2012) agrees that the Revolution was a watershed but a narrower one, working through Parliament's control of taxes and new borrowing and through ministerial responsibility, while property rights at home were little affected. [[c-cox2012]] Steven Pincus and James Robinson argue that the Revolution created very few new formal rules, and that its most significant changes were de facto rather than written into law. [[c-pincus-robinson]]

pages.title: North America to 1750
pages.sub: New Mexico, New France, Virginia and New England
pages.lede: Between 1607 and 1610 England, France and Spain founded Jamestown, Quebec and Santa Fe. Native nations made treaties and fought wars, from Plymouth's treaty with Massasoit to King Philip's War and the Pueblo Revolt, and in 1619 captive Africans reached Virginia, a date whose place in the American story is still argued over.
body: Pedro de Peralta founded Santa Fe as the capital of New Mexico in 1610. [[c-santafe]] Spanish missionaries burned the Pueblos' kivas, masks and other sacred objects, and on 10 August 1680 Popé led a full-scale revolt; the Spaniards sheltered in the Palace of the Governors and then fled, leaving about 400 dead, among them 21 priests. [[c-pueblo-revolt]] The Pueblos stayed free until 1692, when the Spanish reconquest of New Mexico began. Santa Fe itself was retaken by force in December 1693. [[c-pueblo-1692]]

Samuel de Champlain began the settlement of Quebec in 1608, and in New France the fur trade remained everyone's chief concern except the missionaries'. [[c-quebec]] The Haudenosaunee, 'the people of the longhouse', were a confederacy of five nations that the English called the Six Nations after the Tuscarora joined in 1722. [[c-haudenosaunee]] When the League was founded is disputed, and proposed dates vary widely, among them Lewis Henry Morgan's 1400-1450 and W. M. Beauchamp's 1600. Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields dated it by a solar eclipse to 31 August 1142, but David Henige finds 'no serious evidence' for that date. [[c-league-date]]

Jamestown, settled in May 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in North America; it lived through the 'Starving Time' of 1609-10, and in July 1619 its governor called the first representative assembly. [[c-jamestown]] That year the '20 and odd' Africans arrived, captives seized by the English warship White Lion from a Portuguese slave ship (on the Atlantic slave trade, see 13.7). [[c-1619-arrival]] Virginia recognised slavery in statute law in 1662 and codified its slave laws in 1705. [[c-virginia-law]] In December 2019 five historians asked the New York Times to correct the 1619 Project's claim that protecting slavery was a main reason for the American Revolution. The Times defended it, but in March 2020 it changed the passage to say that this was a primary motivation for 'some of the colonists'. Adam Serwer argues that the quarrel is really about national identity. [[c-1619-debate]]

At Plymouth, founded in 1620, in the first winter half the Mayflower's passengers and crew died of disease and malnutrition; the treaty with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, signed in March 1621, held until after his death in 1661. [[c-plymouth]] In 1675 war broke out between Native Americans and the English settlers and their Indian allies; named after his son Metacom, whom the English called Philip, King Philip's War was per capita one of the bloodiest conflicts in American history. [[c-kpw]] Some 800 English died and a third of New England's English towns were burned and abandoned; among Native people about 2,000 died of wounds, 3,000 of disease or starvation, and 1,000 were sold into slavery. [[c-kpw-toll]]
